114	## Overrides Pattern
115	
116	All customizations live in `overrides/` mirroring the structure of `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/`. Never edit `node_modules/`.
117	
118	**Minimise custom code.** When implementing Zimmermann's design and layout, stay as close to the base PWA Kit implementation as possible. Style changes (CSS, Chakra props, theme tokens) are always expected and need no confirmation. Structural changes — restructuring components, altering data flow, or significantly deviating from base template behaviour — must be confirmed with the user before proceeding.
119	
120	**Before any change:** check whether the file exists in `overrides/`. If not, create the override:
121	
122	1. Copy from `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/` to the mirrored path in `overrides/`.
123	2. Rename `.js`/`.jsx` → `.ts`/`.tsx`. Replace `PropTypes` with TypeScript `type` definitions. Add explicit types to all parameters, return values, and props. Use Commerce SDK types (`commerce-sdk-isomorphic`, `@salesforce/commerce-sdk-react`) where available. No `as any` or `// @ts-ignore`.
124	3. Verify `npx tsc --noEmit` passes with zero errors.
125	4. **Stop. Present the converted file to the user and wait for approval before making any functional changes.**

161	
162	Content types (schema) are never created manually in the Contentful web app. They are defined in code and synced via a script. This makes schema changes reviewable, repeatable, and team-safe.

166	- `scripts/contentful/sync.js` — runner: upserts (creates or updates) and publishes every content type in the definitions directory

170	
171	1. Add a definition file to `scripts/contentful/content-types/<contentTypeId>.js` (see existing files for shape)

176	```
177	npm run sync:contentful
178	```

258

260	
261	The SSR layer in `overrides/app/ssr.js` uses **Node's native `fetch`**, which is backed by `undici`. Undici's `dispatcher` option (the per-call `dispatcher` option on individual `fetch()` invocations) allows each upstream origin to be given its own connection pool with an independent cap. 262	
263	```ts
264	import { Pool } from 'undici';
265	
266	// 1. Create isolated pools for specific origins
267	const checkoutPool = new Pool('https://api.checkout-service.com', {
268	  connections: 10, // Hard limit of 10 concurrent connections to this origin
269	  timeout: 8000,
270	});
271	
272	// 2. Use them explicitly in your fetch calls inside ssr.js
273	async function getCheckoutMetadata() {
274	  return await fetch('https://api.checkout-service.com/v1/metadata', {
275	    dispatcher: checkoutPool, // Safely isolated!
276	  });
277	}
278	```

Separate from `sfcc-scapi` because a checkout traffic spike must not consume SLAS connections.                                                                                               |

GiveX balance calls carry payment credentials in the POST body — a slow MuleSoft response must not hold connections open and starve other pools. Highest cap reflects the broadest call surface. |

# Architecture

_Key technical decisions, stack overview, overrides pattern, component organisation, and key paths. Update this file when the stack changes, a new integration is added, or a structural decision is made._

Production storefront for www.zimmermann.com — multi-locale, multi-currency, eight storefronts across six regions (AU, US, UK, EU, HK, ME), with both EU and US each split into two storefronts (domestic + international).

## Pre-Build Decisions

These decisions affect tooling, CI, and code shape that's hard to retrofit later. Status as of 2026-05-29.

| #   | Decision                     | Status                                 |
| --- | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| 1   | Browser & device matrix      | ✅ Confirmed (informal)                |
| 2   | Accessibility manual testing | 🟡 Partial — vendor info pending       |
| 3   | Performance budgets          | ✅ Confirmed (informal)                |
| 4   | Client-side error reporting  | ⚪ Accepted risk — no tool             |
| 5   | Feature-flag tool            | ⚪ Accepted risk — Optimizely Web only |
| 6   | Translation fallback chain   | 🟡 Partial — Brand/Legal pending       |

### #1 — Browser & device matrix ✅

**Mobile perf-test floor:** current OS version −2 on iPhone and Android (iOS 17+, Android 14+), verified via BrowserStack Automate. `package.json` browserslist aligned to match.
**Desktop matrix** ([.browserstack.yml](../../.browserstack.yml)): Chrome + Safari (macOS Sonoma), Firefox + Edge (Windows 11) — all latest.

### #2 — Accessibility 🟡

**Target:** WCAG 2.2 AA, at least 2.1 AA. **Automated:** axe-core in Vitest + Playwright; Storybook a11y addon; Lighthouse CI a11y ≥0.90 ([lighthouserc.js](../../lighthouserc.js)). **Manual:** client's existing a11y vendor.
**Pending:** vendor name, screen-reader/browser matrix, audit cadence, remediation owner.

### #3 — Performance budgets ✅

**Client-mandated:** **LCP ≤ 2s** at p75 mobile, plus Lighthouse Performance ≥ 0.80, Accessibility ≥ 0.90, Best Practices ≥ 0.90. These are the only performance numbers in the signed TSD (§9).
**Other CWV (internal working defaults, not client-mandated):** INP ≤ 200ms · CLS ≤ 0.1. Lighthouse mobile defaults at p75.
**CI gate (SIT gate):** Lighthouse CI (`@lhci/cli`) asserts the Lighthouse score floors above, plus a >5pt trend-drop gate (LHCI server required). SEO intentionally not asserted. Runs on every PR to `develop` ([`digital-sit.yml`](../../.github/workflows/digital-sit.yml)), deploys to the **Dev** tier on merge — treat its numbers as a **regression indicator**, not the contractual measurement.
**Contractual measurement:** Client-mandated LCP and Lighthouse numbers are validated on **Stage** — the prod-mimicking tier (same MRT bundle size class, same CDN/edge configuration, same SFCC realm tier as production). The Dev tier is slower and further from the edge, so its absolute numbers will be worse — that is expected and not a sign-off concern. Full environment topology in [tsd-architecture.md §14.1](./temp/tsd-architecture.md).
**Bundle ceilings — internal CI policy, NOT client requirements:** `main.js` 180 kB · `vendor.js` 250 kB · `main.css` 50 kB (`bundlesize` in `package.json`). (These were set as aspirational targets early in the project. As of the last measurement the actual sizes are well above these ceilings (`main.js` ~352 kB, `vendor.js` ~2 MB) before any optimisation pass — the ceilings need to be re-baselined against measured size + a growth-only headroom (e.g. current + 10–15%) once a baseline pass is done.) Their purpose is regression detection, not a client-facing commitment.
**Third-party script weight:** uncapped — tight LCP is the de-facto constraint. See AGENTS.md > Performance for the deferral rule.

### #6 — Translation fallback 🟡

[regional.md](./prd/regional.md) REG-046: "English is the site-wide fallback." Doesn't disambiguate `en-eu` vs `en`, nor split by content type.
**Pending Brand/Legal decision** on the rule per content type:

| Content type | Suggested chain          | Why                                          |
| ------------ | ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------- |
| UI strings   | `fr-eu` → `en-eu` → `en` | Universal meaning                            |
| Editorial    | `fr-eu` → `en-eu` → hide | Avoid half-translated pages                  |
| Product copy | `fr-eu` → `en-eu` → hide | Care/sizing are region-specific (regulatory) |

REG-047 (Contentful↔Transperfect↔SFCC workflow) remains separately TBC.

### Accepted risks

**#4 — No client-side error reporting.** JS errors in customer browsers (e.g. Adyen iframe failure on a specific iOS Safari version) are invisible to the team; detection relies on support tickets. Revisit post-launch if checkout completion dips unexplained.

**#5 — No feature-flag tool.** Optimizely Web Experimentation ([analytics.md](./prd/analytics.md) AAB-004) covers analytics A/B. Note (confirmed 09-06): Optimizely is **not** a GTM tag — the PWA loads its script directly in the page head (US storefront only, single snippet across environments, before render to avoid flicker), Didomi-gated. Progressive rollout, social login dark-launch, and August-2026 payment-method gating will be handled via deploy timing and branch merges — no instant kill-switch, no % rollouts.

## Frontend Stack

### Bundled by PWA Kit

| Layer                        | Library                                               | Notes                                                                                 |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Base framework               | PWA Kit v3+                                           | Salesforce storefront foundation                                                      |
| UI framework                 | React 18 + Chakra UI                                  | Component library + theme system                                                      |
| Routing                      | React Router v6                                       |                                                                                       |
| Server/async state           | TanStack Query (via `@salesforce/commerce-sdk-react`) | All SFCC data fetching                                                                |
| i18n                         | react-intl                                            | Translations in `translations/`                                                       |
| Build + dev server           | Webpack 5 (via `pwa-kit-dev`)                         |                                                                                       |
| Build + test runner (legacy) | Jest (via `pwa-kit-dev test`)                         | `jest.config.js` — kept for PWA Kit internals; superseded by Vitest for project tests |

### Project additions

| Layer                                  | Library                                        | Notes                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Type safety                            | TypeScript strict mode                         | `tsconfig.json`                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Component explorer + interaction tests | Storybook 8                                    | `storybook dev -p 6006`; `play` functions are the primary tool for component-level interaction testing                                                                                                              |
| Storybook a11y addon                   | `@storybook/addon-a11y`                        | Component-level accessibility checks during development and in Storybook test runs                                                                                                                                  |
| Unit test runner                       | Vitest                                         | `vitest.config.ts`; replaces `pwa-kit-dev test` for project tests                                                                                                                                                   |
| Accessibility testing                  | axe-core (via `vitest-axe` / `axe-playwright`) | Automated WCAG checks in unit and E2E layers; see Pre-Build Decisions #2 for outstanding items                                                                                                                      |
| E2E tests (planned)                    | Playwright                                     | Not yet configured                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Forms + validation                     | react-hook-form + zod                          | Not yet installed; add when checkout/account work begins                                                                                                                                                            |
| Global UI state                        | Zustand                                        | For shared state that outgrows Context (multi-step flows, drawer state, etc.). **SSR note:** initialise store per-request — never as a module singleton — to prevent state leaking across server-rendered requests. |

### External services

Salesforce Commerce Cloud, Contentful Studio CMS, Global-e (international checkout + server-side pricing/catalogue feed — PRC-34..43 sign-off pending), Didomi (consent), GTM hosted on Addingwell (data layer + downstream tag loading via Tell No Lies). Full integration map below.

## Environments

Six-tier topology spans **Local → Dev → SIT → Stage → UAT → Prod**. Each tier (other than Local) has its own SFCC realm, Contentful environment, and MuleSoft connections. Ownership splits across three zones — Digital, IT/NewStore, and Shared (Digital + Business).

| #   | Tier            | Owner         | Purpose                                                                      | Third-party availability                                              | Deploy trigger                                                              |
| --- | --------------- | ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | **Local**       | Digital       | Feature build on developer machines                                          | All services mocked (MSW stubs)                                       | `npm start`                                                                 |
| 2   | **Dev**         | Digital       | Integrated digital testing across all 6 storefronts, independent of NewStore | MuleSoft STG · NewStore Dev · Omneo STG · Narvar stub · Adyen sandbox | Merge to `develop`                                                          |
| 3   | **SIT**         | IT / NewStore | NewStore SIT and regression on its own cadence                               | NewStore STG · MuleSoft STG · Narvar STG · AP21 test                  | NewStore release cadence (parallel lane, non-blocking for Digital releases) |
| 4   | **Stage** (E2E) | Shared        | End-to-end testing with all third parties live; time-boxed booked windows    | NewStore STG · MuleSoft STG · Omneo STG · Narvar STG · Adyen sandbox  | Booked 2-week window                                                        |
| 5   | **UAT**         | Shared        | Business acceptance across all 6 regions                                     | NewStore STG · Narvar STG · Omneo STG · Adyen sandbox                 | Business approval gate                                                      |
| 6   | **Prod**        | Live          | Production; AU canary then flag-flip to remaining regions                    | NewStore PROD · MuleSoft PROD · Omneo PROD · Narvar PROD · Adyen PROD | Release manager + canary gate                                               |

**Stage** is the contractual performance-test environment referenced under [Pre-Build Decisions #3](#3--performance-budgets-) — it mirrors production infrastructure (same MRT bundle class, CDN/edge configuration, SFCC realm tier).

**QA workflow** ([`qa.yml`](../.github/workflows/qa.yml)) runs on every PR to `develop` and `release/**`: Vitest unit tests and Storybook interaction + `@storybook/addon-a11y` component-level accessibility checks (`storybook test --ci`), in parallel. Code-correctness checks that run before any environment is involved.

**SIT gate** ([`digital-sit.yml`](../.github/workflows/digital-sit.yml)) runs on push/PR to `release/**`: Playwright `p0` specs, bundle-size check, MuleSoft contract tests, Lighthouse CI thresholds, LHCI trend gate. Environment-dependent checks against the deployed Dev tier. On merge to `develop` it also deploys to Dev. Production deploys are gated on a clean SIT gate run plus stakeholder approval through Stage and UAT.

**MRT targets** in [mobify.config.js](../mobify.config.js) map one-to-one to the topology: `dev | sit | stage | uat | production`. `ENVIRONMENT_NAME` (`local | dev | sit | stage | uat | prod`) is the per-tier tag emitted to Sentry, New Relic, and GTM.

## SSR Requirement (DMU-030)

Server-side rendering is **mandatory** for product, category, and content pages (DMU-030, signed off). PWA Kit's SSR pipeline must be preserved — do not introduce client-only patterns (e.g. `typeof window !== 'undefined'` short-circuits, client-only data fetching on first paint, or `next/dynamic`-style `{ ssr: false }`) on these page types. Any componentry that cannot render on the server must be gated behind a hydration-safe boundary that still emits SEO-relevant markup on the server.

## Overrides Pattern

All customizations live in `overrides/` mirroring the structure of `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/`. Never edit `node_modules/`.

**Minimise custom code.** When implementing Zimmermann's design and layout, stay as close to the base PWA Kit implementation as possible. Style changes (CSS, Chakra props, theme tokens) are always expected and need no confirmation. Structural changes — restructuring components, altering data flow, or significantly deviating from base template behaviour — must be confirmed with the user before proceeding.

**Before any change:** check whether the file exists in `overrides/`. If not, create the override:

1. Copy from `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/` to the mirrored path in `overrides/`.
2. Rename `.js`/`.jsx` → `.ts`/`.tsx`. Replace `PropTypes` with TypeScript `type` definitions. Add explicit types to all parameters, return values, and props. Use Commerce SDK types (`commerce-sdk-isomorphic`, `@salesforce/commerce-sdk-react`) where available. No `as any` or `// @ts-ignore`.
3. Verify `npx tsc --noEmit` passes with zero errors.
4. **Stop. Present the converted file to the user and wait for approval before making any functional changes.**

## New vs. Override Components

- **Overriding a base template component:** copy from `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/` to the mirrored path in `overrides/` (see Overrides Pattern above).
- **Brand-new components** (no base template equivalent): create them in `overrides/app/components/custom/`.

## Key Paths

- **Country/locale/currency mappings:** `overrides/app/config/countries.ts` — single source of truth for URL slugs, locales, currencies, shipping countries, Global-e flag, and boutique regions. When adding a market also update `config/sites.js`.
- **Contentful config:** `overrides/app/config/contentful.ts` — always render locale-specific content using Contentful's native localisation fields. Gate preview/draft content behind a server-side check; never expose draft content in production.
- **Theme / design tokens:** `overrides/app/theme/` — `index.ts` composes the theme; brand tokens live in `foundation/` (colour, fonts, typography, gridSystem, spacing — Tier 1, UI Designer owned); per-component overrides live one file each in `components/` (e.g. `header.ts`, `listMenu.ts` — Tier 2). Register a new component override in `components/index.ts`.

## Cross-Storefront Session & Basket Scope

All eight storefronts are path-prefixed on a single first-party domain and share one SFCC realm with shared customer data. The `httpOnly` SLAS refresh-token cookie set by the SSR layer is therefore presented on every storefront prefix — no cross-domain SSO bridge is needed. SLAS tokens are channel-scoped, so the SSR layer re-initialises the SLAS context per storefront; a registered shopper is silently re-recognised across a storefront switch (shared customer record), while a guest session is site-scoped and does not carry over. **The basket deliberately does not transfer across storefronts** — baskets are site-scoped and priced in the storefront's own currency/pricebook, so a shopper switching storefront starts a fresh basket. Carrying a basket across a currency boundary would produce incorrect pricing. The Global-e checkout handoff is a separate session boundary (Global-e owns its hosted checkout in full). ## Blast-Radius Mitigation

Multiple upstream integrations (SFCC, MuleSoft/Omneo, Global-e, Narvar, Contentful, Didomi, Inside Chat) mean a failure or attack targeting one service must not cascade. A PWA-relevant mitigation can be done in the SSR layer.

The SSR layer in `overrides/app/ssr.js` uses **Node's native `fetch`**, which is backed by `undici`. Undici's `dispatcher` option (the per-call `dispatcher` option on individual `fetch()` invocations) allows each upstream origin to be given its own connection pool with an independent cap. This prevents a slow or flooded integration (e.g. checkout APIs) from exhausting connections for unrelated origins (e.g. Contentful, JWKS).

```ts
import { Pool } from 'undici';

// 1. Create isolated pools for specific origins
const checkoutPool = new Pool('https://api.checkout-service.com', {
  connections: 10, // Hard limit of 10 concurrent connections to this origin
  timeout: 8000,
});

// 2. Use them explicitly in your fetch calls inside ssr.js
async function getCheckoutMetadata() {
  return await fetch('https://api.checkout-service.com/v1/metadata', {
    dispatcher: checkoutPool, // Safely isolated!
  });
}
```

# Upstream update policy

How we handle new releases of `@salesforce/retail-react-app` (and the surrounding PWA Kit SDKs).

## Principle

**Bump opportunistically — not on a schedule.** Stay on the current version unless a release contains something we actually care about.

Reasons to bump:
- **Security** — CVE fix, dependency patch with a known vulnerability, advisory we are exposed to.
- **SDK** — a change in `pwa-kit-runtime`, `pwa-kit-react-sdk`, `commerce-sdk-react`, or `pwa-kit-dev` that affects code we depend on (SSR, routing, hooks we use, build pipeline).
- **Bug fix or feature we have been waiting for** — a fix to behaviour we currently work around, or a feature that lets us delete custom code, or will help us on implementing a planned feature.

Reasons **not** to bump:
- A release with only template/UI changes that we have already overridden.
- A release whose changelog touches packages or paths we do not use.
- "It's been a while."

## Discipline

When the upstream-release-watch workflow opens a tracking issue (see [.github/workflows/upstream-release-watch.yml](../.github/workflows/upstream-release-watch.yml)):

1. Open the linked release notes.
2. Skim for the three categories above.
3. If nothing relevant, close the issue with a one-line reason and update `Reviewed up to` in [.docs/memory/upstreamBaseline.md](memory/upstreamBaseline.md). **Do not bump.**
4. If something relevant, bump — then update `Current` and `Reviewed up to` together.

## What we do not do

- **No drift detection script.** We do not diff our `overrides/` against the upstream template on a schedule. Drift is the *point* of the overrides pattern.
- **No two-track review.** There is no separate "SDK package review" vs "template code skim." If we bump, we bump; the changelog tells us what to test.
- **No bump because it's been N weeks.** Time alone is not a reason.

## Related

- Current baseline: [.docs/memory/upstreamBaseline.md](memory/upstreamBaseline.md)
- Watch workflow: [.github/workflows/upstream-release-watch.yml](../.github/workflows/upstream-release-watch.yml)
- CI security gate (once CI lands): `npm audit --audit-level=high` — fail on new highs only.

lastPrompt: what would be the implications if there is a move towards the new version of the pwa kita into react 19 instead of 18, router 7 instead of 6, and tailwind+shadcn instead of chakra

content.text:
No existing mention of Tailwind, shadcn, React 19, or Router 7 anywhere in the repo — this is genuinely new ground, not something already scoped. One thing to pin down first, since it changes the shape of the answer:

**Is this an upstream-driven bump (Salesforce ships a new PWA Kit major version with these) or an independent fork away from what PWA Kit gives you?** They carry very different risk profiles.

## If Salesforce ships it (upstream bump)

- **React 19** is the low-risk piece — mostly a dependency-compat sweep (Contentful SDKs, Storybook packages, the existing `package.json` `overrides` block that already force-pins `react`/`react-dom` to `^18.2.0` for `@salesforce/storefront-next-runtime` would need re-examining).
- **Router 7 is the sleeper risk.** PWA Kit's SSR pipeline (`overrides/app/ssr.js`, `overrides/app/ssr/`, `worker/main.js`, `mobify.config.js`) is custom Node/Express-adjacent plumbing Salesforce built around Router 6 — and per Hard Rule #4, those files are the *one* category Zimmermann can never touch even with owner approval. If Router 7 support means Salesforce re-architected that SSR contract, you're entirely dependent on their migration; there's no local workaround.
- Per `upstreamPolicy.md`, you wouldn't bump for either reason alone — only if the release also fixes something you're blocked on or lets you delete workaround code. Worth checking actual release notes (`upstream-release-watch` workflow) rather than planning against an assumed version.

## Tailwind + shadcn is the bigger call, independent of the above

If you're a PWA Kit developer and are building a Storefront Next storefront, learn about the differences in the technologies and architecture used in PWA Kit and Storefront Next. Storefront Next keeps the same B2C Commerce backend model as PWA Kit (SCAPI, SLAS, and Managed Runtime), but it shifts implementation patterns across the stack. The storefront architecture shifts from a client-heavy, hook-driven architecture in PWA Kit to a server-first architecture built on React Router 7, Vite, and TypeScript in Storefront Next.

## Differences in Project Configuration and the Development Workflow

The PWA Kit and Storefront Next are structured, configured, built, and deployed differently. Migrate a custom Webpack-based workflow in PWA Kit to a more convention-driven Vite and TypeScript workflow in Storefront Next.

### Project Structure

PWA Kit organizes most app code under `app/` with centralized route definitions and explicit runtime entry files. Storefront Next shifts to `src/`, file-based routes, and framework conventions around root and route modules. The outcome is a more convention-driven layout with clearer boundaries for routes, providers, middleware, and adapters.

→ [Project Structure Differences with PWA Kit](/docs/commerce/b2c-commerce/guide/sfnext-pwa-project-structure.html)

### Project Configuration

PWA Kit uses JavaScript configuration with looser runtime validation and flatter structures. Storefront Next introduces typed config definitions, structured namespaces, and an environment-variable override model designed for safer server-client separation. Access patterns also become more context-aware on the server and hook-based in React components.

→ [Project Configuration Differences with PWA Kit](/docs/commerce/b2c-commerce/guide/sfnext-pwa-project-config.html)

### Build Tools

PWA Kit relies on Webpack, Babel, and Jest with multiple build concerns split across separate configs. PWA Kit supports TypeScript optionally through Babel while Storefront Next has TypeScript as a first-class citizen with strict mode enabled. Storefront Next standardizes on Vite, Vitest, and TypeScript-first configuration, which reduces config complexity and speeds up local iteration through faster startup and hot updates. Code splitting and bundle analysis also become more route- and chunk-oriented by default.

→ [Build System Differences with PWA Kit](/docs/commerce/b2c-commerce/guide/sfnext-pwa-build-tools.html)

### Development Workflow

PWA Kit development is driven by Webpack dev tooling and JavaScript-centric config. Storefront Next uses Vite and TypeScript for a faster, more integrated workflow with tighter feedback loops and stronger type safety. Operationally, teams typically see faster local startup, faster HMR, and more consistent tooling across dev/build/test tasks.

→ [Development Workflow Differences with PWA Kit](/docs/commerce/b2c-commerce/guide/sfnext-pwa-dev-workflow.html)

### Deployment

PWA Kit uses a traditional Webpack-based development server with configuration spread across multiple files. Storefront Next leverages Vite for faster development with native ESM, instant HMR, and type-safe configuration. The shift to Vite provides a more modern developer experience with faster feedback loops and better tooling integration.

→ [Deployment Differences with PWA Kit](/docs/commerce/b2c-commerce/guide/sfnext-pwa-deployment.html)

## Differences in Data Fetching, State Management, Storage, and Rendering

The runtime data and app state in PWA Kit is a client-heavy model while it’s a server-first model in Storefront Next. Learn about the rendering, caching, and session handling changes in Storefront Next that affect performance, security, and migration strategy.

### Data Fetching, Suspense, and Loading States

PWA Kit follows a fetch-on-render model where hooks request data during component render and expose manual loading flags. Storefront Next follows fetch-then-render with route loaders that gather data before component rendering, enabling Suspense and streaming patterns more naturally. This moves data concerns out of presentation components and simplifies loading orchestration.

PWA Kit typically handles loading imperatively with `isLoading` checks and manual fallbacks. Storefront Next uses React Suspense and promise-based route data consumption for declarative loading boundaries. This mechanism enables finer-grained streaming and less repetitive loading logic. To migrate to Storefront Next, refactor conditional loading branches into an explicit boundary or fallback design.

→ [Data Fetching and Loading States Differences with PWA Kit](/docs/commerce/b2c-commerce/guide/sfnext-pwa-data-fetching.html)

### State Management

While PWA Kit employs a stateless server architecture paired with TanStack Query for client-side caching, Storefront Next uses HTTP cookies for session persistence.

PWA Kit is stateless on the server side — all pages are server-rendered from the perspective of an unauthenticated (guest) shopper. On the client side, PWA Kit relies on TanStack Query (formerly React Query) as its primary mechanism for caching API responses and managing asynchronous state, supplemented by React Context for local state propagation.

Storefront Next uses HTTP cookies to persist authentication and basket state across requests, and React Context for client-side state management. The framework is unopinionated about state management beyond these defaults; developers are free to integrate the state management solution of their choice and customize the project to fit their requirements.

→ [State Management Differences with PWA Kit](/docs/commerce/b2c-commerce/guide/sfnext-pwa-state-management.html)

### Basket Management

PWA Kit and Storefront Next both use SCAPI baskets, but they differ in where basket state is managed and when full basket data is hydrated. Storefront Next emphasizes middleware-driven basket snapshots and loader/action-based updates with lazy hydration by default.

→ [Basket Management Differences with PWA Kit](/docs/commerce/b2c-commerce/guide/sfnext-pwa-basket-management.html)

### Rendering

PWA Kit SSR is Express-oriented with React Query hydration and optional island-style hydration controls. Storefront Next uses React Router framework SSR with loader-driven data flow, middleware chains, and native streaming/Suspense patterns. This rendering model reduces SSR boilerplate and aligns rendering behavior more directly with route modules.

→ [Server-Side Rendering (SSR) Differences with PWA Kit](/docs/commerce/b2c-commerce/guide/sfnext-pwa-rendering.html)

### Storage and Sessions

PWA Kit auth/session data often spans both server and client, including localStorage token usage in common patterns. Storefront Next centralizes auth on the server and uses `httpOnly` cookies as the primary session/token mechanism. This mechanism improves security posture and SSR consistency by reducing client-side token handling.

→ [Storage and Sessions Differences with PWA Kit](/docs/commerce/b2c-commerce/guide/sfnext-pwa-storage-sessions.html)

## Differences in API Integration and Routing

Find out how API calls, server handlers, and route definitions are organized in each storefront architecture. Transition from component-level hooks and centralized routing in PWA Kit to loader and action patterns, and file-based routing.

### API Integration

In PWA Kit, API usage is centered on `@salesforce/commerce-sdk-react` hooks and provider-based auth/caching inside components. In Storefront Next, API calls move into route loaders and actions through generated Salesforce B2C Commerce API (SCAPI) clients based on OpenAPI specs. The APIs are provided in the `@salesforce/storefront-next-runtime/scapi` package. Auth is applied through middleware and cache behavior controlled by router revalidation. The result is a thinner client runtime and clearer separation between read and write operations.

→ [API Integration Differences with PWA Kit](/docs/commerce/b2c-commerce/guide/sfnext-pwa-api-integration.html)

### Server Routes

PWA Kit server routes are typically centralized as Express handlers in SSR server code. Storefront Next replaces that with file-based resource routes, and loader and action handlers using standard Web `Request`/`Response` APIs. This routing approach distributes server behavior across route modules and aligns API endpoints with routing conventions.

→ [Server Routes Differences with PWA Kit](/docs/commerce/b2c-commerce/guide/sfnext-pwa-server-routes.html)

### Routing

PWA Kit uses React Router 5 with programmatic route arrays and manual splitting patterns. Storefront Next uses React Router 7 file-based routing with native nested layouts, typed loaders and actions, and automatic route-level splitting. Migrating generally means converting centralized route configuration into route files and moving route data logic into exports.

→ [Routing Differences with PWA Kit](/docs/commerce/b2c-commerce/guide/sfnext-pwa-routing.html)

## Differences in Styling, Components, Static Assets, and SEO

Check out front-end implementation differences between PWA Kit and Storefront Next, including UI composition, styling systems, asset handling, and metadata patterns. Map Chakra and PropTypes-era patterns in PWA Kit to the TypeScript-first and utility-class approach in Storefront Next.

### Styling

PWA Kit styling is largely Chakra CSS-in-JS with prop-based responsive and variant systems. Storefront Next styling centers on Tailwind utility classes, CSS variables, and class-variant composition. The migration is primarily a syntax and architecture shift from style props/theme objects to utility classes and typed variant helpers.

→ [Styling Differences with PWA Kit](/docs/commerce/b2c-commerce/guide/sfnext-pwa-styling.html)

### Components

PWA Kit components are typically JavaScript + PropTypes with Chakra primitives and style props. Storefront Next components are TypeScript-first and composed from Radix/shadcn patterns with utility-class styling and CVA-based variants. The main shift is from runtime styling and theme objects to compile-time class composition and typed component contracts.

→ [Component Differences with PWA Kit](/docs/commerce/b2c-commerce/guide/sfnext-pwa-components.html)

### Static Assets

PWA Kit uses Webpack-era asset helpers, sprite-based icon patterns, and custom responsive image utilities. Storefront Next adopts Vite-native asset resolution, direct public paths and imports, and component-based responsive image handling with modern preload behavior. Teams typically replace helper-heavy patterns with simpler import and path conventions.

→ [Static Assets Differences with PWA Kit](/docs/commerce/b2c-commerce/guide/sfnext-pwa-static-assets.html)

### SEO and Metadata

PWA Kit commonly uses `react-helmet` and supports dynamic API-driven meta tags in current implementations. Storefront Next uses the built-in React Router head/meta capabilities.

→ [SEO and Metadata Differences with PWA Kit](/docs/commerce/b2c-commerce/guide/sfnext-pwa-seo-metadata.html)

That migration doc is describing a full re-platform, not a version bump — but the timing question matters more than the technical diff here, so let me frame both.

## This project is catching it at the cheapest possible moment

Per `.docs/memory/projectState.md`, you're still in **Detailed Design phase — "no production build has started beyond scaffolding."** Concretely: 50 override files total, 8 touching Chakra, 5 touching `commerce-sdk-react`, 0 E2E specs, 2 Storybook stories. Only the header and theme foundation are meaningfully built. Every third-party integration (Global-e, Adyen, MuleSoft, Omneo, Didomi, NewStore, GiveX, Narvar, Google Maps, Avalara, Inside Chat...) is listed as **"Not started."** Full multi-site routing across the 8 storefronts is also still pending. That's the opposite of "this is a big ask" — there's almost nothing to unwind yet.

## What would actually need rework

- **Design system** — `overrides/app/theme/foundation/` (Tier 1, UI-designer-owned) already has Figma tokens finalised (`colour.ts`, `fonts.ts`, `typography.ts`, `gridSystem.ts`, `spacing.ts`) plus the header built against them. Chakra's theme-object model → Tailwind config + CVA variants is a genuine re-expression, not a port — but it's currently only 4 component-theme files + foundation + one header component. Small now; grows fast once PDP/PLP/Cart/Checkout land.
- **Data & session model** — the bigger shift. The 7 Tier-1 commerce hooks (`use-current-basket`, `use-current-customer`, `use-refresh-token`, `use-multi-site`, etc.) are built around client-side TanStack Query + hooks; Storefront Next moves this to route loaders/actions against generated SCAPI clients, with auth centralized server-side via `httpOnly` cookies instead of the current pattern. This is the highest-value change security-wise (matches this project's own no-client-side-secrets bias) but touches every data path, not just styling.
- **SSR layer** — `overrides/app/ssr/` already has real engineering in it (`connectionPools.ts` for undici blast-radius isolation, `contentSecurityPolicy.ts`, `slasTokens.ts`, `marketingCloud.ts`) built Express-style. Storefront Next's loader/middleware SSR model means re-architecting these, not copying them.
- **Governance docs** — `AGENTS.md`, `frozenFiles.md`, `protectedFiles.md`, and CODEOWNERS are all written in terms of PWA Kit's file layout. A framework swap means rewriting the tier model itself against `src/` + file-based routes — and per this repo's own rules, that's Tier 1 governance content requiring **both squad leads + Integration lead** sign-off. That's a structural reason this can't be an engineering-only call.
- **Testing** — low cost either way: Vitest carries over conceptually, and there's no E2E debt yet. Storybook/Playwright selector strategy (role/label-based, per `testing.md`) mostly survives a markup change since it's semantic, not structural.

One aside: the migration doc says "PWA Kit uses React Router 5," but `architecture.md` has this project on v6 already — a minor sign the generic doc doesn't perfectly track this repo's specific versions, worth keeping in mind when reading the other linked pages too.

## Recommendation

If Storefront Next is genuinely the direction Salesforce/the client wants, **the window to decide is before Global-e, Adyen, MuleSoft, and multi-site routing get built** — every one of those is currently a blank slate, and all of them get dramatically more expensive to re-platform once written against PWA Kit's hook/Express model. The tradeoff is that it does mean re-doing the small amount of signed-off Figma/theme work already done, and it's not a decision I'd make from this chat — it needs both squad leads and the Integration lead in the room together, per this project's own governance rules, ideally before the next sprint's integration work starts. Want me to draft a comparison memo for that conversation, or hold here?
